items.t: Trump threatens ‘tremendous penalties’ on US tech firms building datacenters abroad
items.s: President Donald Trump said on Friday that American tech companies building datacenters outside the US would face “tremendous penalties”, though he offered no details. He made the remarks at a wide-ranging White House press conference.
p: Trump said he did not want US companies to build datacenters in other countries, arguing that China would take them if they were allowed to. He told reporters he had not yet informed his own officials about the plan.

At the same briefing, Trump said he would “look into” a report that Iran had been planning to detonate a “dirty bomb” in Washington DC. He described the report as a rumour and said that if Iran did so, “we’re going to fight.”

Trump also backed Vice-President JD Vance, whose comments had blamed Republican losses in the midterm elections on the Iran war. Asked about reports of a rift between them, Trump said Vance’s remark was “a very accurate statement”.

On foreign leaders, Trump spoke warmly about Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping, whom he met at the Apec summit on Thursday. He said he had “fantastic relationships” with both, and was asked whether Putin could be considered a friend given Russia’s close ties to Iran.

On datacenters at home, Trump said Americans should welcome the facilities but that communities should seek payments from developers. “Make them pay your community,” he said, adding that they should not be shut out.

The remarks come as many Americans oppose datacenters being built near their homes. The tech industry has responded by promising fewer government handouts, more transparency and more money for towns that host the facilities.

Separately, the administration on Monday issued new rules restricting remote access to advanced US computing chips, which it said were meant to limit China’s ability to use US chips for training. A House committee said on Wednesday that the US had approved sales of nearly 900,000 chips to China over six months. The chipmaker Nvidia, in which Trump is an investor, has also drawn attention after its chief executive, Jensen Huang, was fired over an affair with a woman who was alleged to be spying for China.
items.cav: The Guardian reports the penalties without any details, and Al Jazeera’s summary describes “a tremendous tax” instead, so the exact measure remains unclear. The dirty bomb report is unverified, and the chip sales figure comes from a House committee rather than a confirmed administration statement.
items.op: Threatening punishment for companies without publishing a rule, a legal basis or a timetable is governance by remark. Businesses and communities deserve to know what the penalties would be before they make decisions that affect jobs and land. Clarity, not bluster, is what should be expected from the White House.

items.t: Trump defends Putin ties and warns data centres must stay in the US
items.s: US President Donald Trump praised his recent trip to China and defended his relationship with Russia’s Vladimir Putin, while warning tech companies against building data centres overseas. The remarks came at a wide-ranging White House news conference on Friday.
p: Trump described Putin as a “friend” during a recent summit that also included Chinese President Xi Jinping. When reporters at a White House briefing asked whether the Russian leader was in fact a friend to the United States, Trump did not give a direct answer. “I can’t speak to America,” he said, before adding that Putin had been “very nice” during the so-called Russia hoax investigation that followed his 2016 presidential campaign.

Trump said he had a very good relationship with Putin, and he linked the comments to Russia’s nuclear weapons capabilities. He also praised the summit as one of the most important international meetings in many years. According to his account, it was the first ever trilateral meeting between the leaders of the United States, Russia and China. He praised what he called a “first of its kind trilateral peace agreement”, although the reporting says no major deals were announced from the meeting.
On Friday, Trump played up his agreement with Putin and Xi to hold future discussions on nuclear proliferation, presenting it as a success of the summit.

The news conference also covered the war involving Iran, which is approaching its 10-month anniversary. Trump accused Tehran of negotiating in bad faith. He said Iran wanted a deal but not one acceptable to him, and that Washington wanted a real agreement rather than a fake one. He did not set out the terms he was seeking.

Several senior officials stood beside him in the briefing room, including Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, both of whom were named as possible 2028 presidential contenders. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Defence Secretary Hegseth and newly appointed White House chief of staff Stephen Miller were also present.

Trump denied he was upset with Vance, who had reportedly blamed the Iran war for the historic midterm losses suffered by Republicans. Trump said Vance’s statement was fine, adding that if asked, he would have said he would do the war again, and that the answer was yes. Vance said the president makes the decisions and that his job was to support him.

Trump warned US technology companies against building new data centres in other countries, saying they would face a “tremendous tax”. He said the country would not allow such facilities abroad because China would take them all, and that penalties would follow for companies that tried. He did not explain how the policy would be enforced and said he had not yet briefed his own officials on it. Al Jazeera said it had contacted the White House for comment and had not received a reply.
items.cav: Trump’s claims about the summit, including that it was the first of its kind and produced a peace agreement, are his own characterisations and are not independently confirmed in the reporting. Vance’s midterm remarks are described second-hand. The data centre policy has no published details, and the White House had not responded at the time of reporting.
items.op: A leader who praises a rival’s personal friendship while promising unexplained penalties for companies owes the public clear rules and clear reasons. Policy announced from a press room, before officials are briefed, is a warning sign for transparency. Governments should set out the terms before they threaten business.

items.t: Trump threatens ban on US firms building data centres overseas
items.s: US President Donald Trump has said American companies will not be allowed to build data centres abroad, threatening a “tremendous tax” on firms that do so. He gave few details, and it remains unclear how such a policy would work.
p: Donald Trump said he would ban US companies from building data centres overseas, according to the BBC. He threatened a “tremendous tax” for technology firms that went ahead anyway. Speaking to reporters at a press briefing after returning from a trip to Asia, he said: “We’re going to keep it all in this country.”

The BBC reported that Trump gave little detail on the potential policy. He said other members of his cabinet were hearing about it for the first time, and he admitted he had not yet raised it with his own team. He linked the idea to China, saying Beijing would otherwise take all such facilities.

The BBC noted that it remains unclear how the policy would be enforced if it were introduced. Large technology companies, including Meta and Google, have already signed agreements to build data centres overseas.

The remarks came after data centres became a central issue in the midterm elections earlier in November. Many Democratic candidates promised tougher regulation of their construction, and concerns about noise pollution and energy consumption helped them win on 3 November, the BBC said.

Trump took a different line on the facilities themselves. He told reporters that communities should “take advantage” of data centres and make the companies pay them, rather than shut them out. He added that many places want them and have energy and other assets to offer.

The announcement also follows a separate move by Washington. On Monday, the US said firms would need a licence to buy advanced computer chips, so officials can monitor whether the chips are used to serve Chinese companies or smuggled into China. The BBC reported that this will affect South East Asian countries that have invested heavily in data centres.

According to the Pew Research Centre, cited by the BBC, there were about 3,000 data centres across the US as of April, with another 1,500 at various stages of approval and construction. Many are in rural areas.

The BBC also reported that Canada has moved to position itself as an alternative location, with less local pushback so far. Meta has broken ground on a data centre in Alberta, and Anthropic has signed a long-term agreement to lease a proposed site in Nova Scotia. In Finland, Google announced a €13bn ($15bn: £11bn) infrastructure investment in September, including funding for three data centres. The BBC said building work on two of them was halted last month over concerns about clearing more than 300 hectares of forest. Trump singled out the Finland project, saying his administration was “not allowing that to happen.”
items.cav: The source is a single BBC report and the policy has not been published or formally defined. The BBC says it is unclear how enforcement would work, and the claim that other officials had not been briefed comes from Trump's own remarks.
items.op: A major economic policy should not be announced through off-the-cuff remarks to reporters. Companies, allies and voters need written rules, legal authority and a clear enforcement mechanism. Until those exist, a threatened “tremendous tax” is a headline, not a policy.

items.t: COP31 enters final phase in Antalya with no deal yet and a draft that omits fossil fuel phaseout
items.s: The UN climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, was running past its scheduled close on Friday with no agreement, after a new draft declaration left out any mention of phasing out fossil fuels. According to DW, talks could continue into the weekend.
p: Delegates from nearly 200 countries gathered in Antalya for the closing stage of the COP31 climate summit, after about two weeks of negotiations. DW reported that countries remain divided on how to tackle global warming.

A new draft declaration does not mention phasing out fossil fuels, which DW describes as the main drivers of climate change. Campaigners quoted by the broadcaster called the omission a step backwards and a clear regression.

Late on Friday, a plenary session began well after its official closing time. Turkish presidency's opening address was partly drowned out by a protester who shouted objections in English, and the chamber applauded.

COP31 President Murat Kurum, who is also Turkey's environment minister, told the plenary that negotiators had been working for days to find common ground and hailed the progress made. The plenary also noted that several of the more ambitious parts of the political declaration were still incomplete. Several national delegates used the session to complain about slow progress, and in some cases what they described as backsliding.

Ethiopia, which will host next year's summit, confirmed its plans during the same session. Foreign minister Gedion Timothewos, who will preside over COP32, described the process as a long-distance race rather than a sprint, and said Addis Ababa would take up the work next year.

DW also reported that the IPCC has put on hold its next series of multi-year scientific assessments, at the urging of countries including Russia, Saudi Arabia and Iran. The broadcaster said the US government has not sent an official delegation, while American lawmakers, mayors and governors travelled to Turkey instead. US President Donald Trump, who has called global warming a hoax, did not send a formal delegation for the second year running.

Uganda's environment minister, Beatrice Atim Anywar, said funding promised by wealthy countries to help with climate impacts has not materialised, and that her country hopes oil and carbon credits will help close the gap.

Victor Menotti of the Demand Climate Justice NGO told DW that European governments appeared to be borrowing negotiating tactics associated with the Trump administration. He accused them of seeking to dilute their responsibilities and of expecting unrealistic commitments from developing countries. He also pointed to Germany's continued subsidies for coal and fossil fuels, and said the wealthier countries should act first.
items.cav: All of the substance comes from a single DW report, and the summit outcome was still unresolved when it was published. The claims about Germany, the US posture and Uganda's funding are attributed to the people quoted and have not been independently checked in these sources.
items.op: A climate deal that avoids naming fossil fuels fails the basic test of what the summit is for. Governments owe their citizens clear commitments and public scrutiny of what they agree to, not vague language settled after midnight. Delegates should put the phaseout back on the table and explain any refusal in public.

items.t: Cop31 talks in Antalya overrun deadline as draft text omits fossil fuels
items.s: Negotiators at the Cop31 summit in Antalya, Turkey, kept working past the planned Friday close, with a draft that makes no reference to fossil fuels at the centre of the dispute.
p: Negotiations at the Cop31 UN climate summit ran past their planned close on Friday, according to The Guardian. Delegates were still disputing a draft agreement that contains no reference to fossil fuels, and several other unresolved questions were slowing progress. The paper understood that a revised text would probably not be ready until Saturday morning.

The wording had moved considerably during the week. An early draft called for faster phase-outs of coal, oil and gas. A shorter version circulated on Thursday removed any mention of those fuels and softened targets on electrification.

Brazil’s national secretary for climate change, Aloisio Lopes Pereira de Melo, summed up the mood by saying “At this point, no one is happy.” Panama’s climate minister, Juan Carlos Navarro, rejected a document that does not mention fossil fuels at all. Eight countries have asked for a clear transition away from fossil fuels to be reinstated, and seven others, including Panama and Belgium, listed issues they consider essential.

Cop insiders, speaking anonymously to the Guardian, said Saudi Arabia was taking an obstructive line. The paper reported that the kingdom wants carbon capture, utilisation and storage to be prominently referenced in the final text, as a way of limiting overshoot of the 1.5C goal set in Paris. Neil Grant of the advisory group Climate Analytics argued that the technology is being written in because fossil fuel interests want it there, calling it a “Trojan horse”.

Observer groups with a formal role in the talks described the process as the “worst Cop ever”. They said none of their priorities had survived the negotiations, and they were especially aggrieved that a just transition mechanism agreed a year earlier had not been advanced.

Ministers from Ghana, Zambia, Senegal, Kenya and Sierra Leone held a press conference on Friday morning. They argued that African countries were being made to bear the costs of a crisis they had not created, and accused wealthier nations of using carbon taxes to keep the continent from turning its mineral resources into industry. Zanetor Agyeman-Rawlings of Ghana, who chairs the African negotiators’ group, said: “We didn’t come here to beg.”

Climate finance remains a major sticking point. A senior EU official said the bloc and its member states had provided €32.3bn from public sources and mobilised €9.3bn in private finance in 2025. Observers have blamed richer countries, the EU among them, for holding back progress on money throughout the week. These EU figures are the official’s own statement and were not checked independently in the article.

Chris Bowen, who is presiding over the talks, defended the process, saying “Well, red lines – that’s how negotiations work.” He added that no one had yet proposed abandoning the effort. The last Cop to end on schedule was held in Italy in 2003, and some earlier sessions have spilled into the following Sunday.
items.cav: Every detail here comes from one Guardian report written on the final day, and the sources do not include the final text or the outcome. The claims about Saudi Arabia rest on anonymous insiders, and the criticism of carbon capture is one expert’s opinion. The EU funding figures are an official’s claim.
items.op: Nearly 200 governments are still divided over whether a climate deal should name the fuel driving the crisis, and that omission is the real test. A text that promises action while leaving fossil fuels out invites distrust. Negotiators should state their objections openly and make clear who is blocking progress.

items.t: Anthropic shares slide back toward IPO price as tech sell-off deepens
items.s: Anthropic’s stock market debut drew strong early interest, but its shares have fallen back toward their offer price as a wider sell-off hits technology stocks. Major US indexes slipped into correction territory on Friday.
p: Anthropic, the maker of the Claude chatbot, rose sharply on its first day of trading on the Nasdaq on Thursday, after raising a record $81bn in its initial public offering. The shares opened at $111.50 and peaked at $115 before ending the day up 17% at $97.17, according to the BBC.

On Friday the stock gave back much of that gain. The BBC reported that it dropped at one point by more than 12% to about $85, close to its IPO price of $83. Al Jazeera put the shares at $87.95 around midday in New York, about 9.5% below Thursday’s close, while still above the offer price of $83.30. The two outlets’ figures reflect different moments in the session.

The fall in Anthropic’s shares came against a broader decline in technology stocks. By mid-afternoon, the S&P 500 was down about 2.8% and the Dow Jones Industrial Average was down more than 1%. Both touched correction territory, which is generally defined as trading 10% or more below a recent high. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite fell more than 4%.

Several large companies also dropped. The BBC reported that Nvidia had fallen more than 11% by the afternoon, with Tesla and SpaceX down more than 6% and Meta down more than 5%. Al Jazeera, citing an earlier point in the day, put Nvidia down nearly 7%, with Meta down almost 4%. Chip makers including AMD and Sandisk also sold off sharply in Al Jazeera’s account.

Analysts quoted in the reports said the IPO had not restored confidence across the sector. Ed Moya of AlphaSense told the BBC that investors were asking how much they were willing to pay for growth, and that Wall Street appeared to be shifting toward demanding stronger cash flow. David Miller of Catalyst Funds told Al Jazeera that investors are “becoming more selective about what they will pay for that growth.”

Markets in Europe and Asia also weakened. The BBC reported that Germany’s Dax closed down 2.6%, while South Korea’s Kospi and Japan’s Nikkei 225 each closed down about 5%. Taiwan’s market fell roughly 6% on Friday, which the BBC said was reported to be its biggest weekly fall since 1990.

Both outlets noted that early volatility is common for newly listed technology firms. Analysts pointed out that Anthropic had no direct listed peers, and comparisons were drawn with SpaceX, whose shares swung sharply after its June debut. Al Jazeera reported that SpaceX rose nearly 50% in its first three days before falling below its IPO price a month later.
items.cav: The sources give different intraday figures for Anthropic and Nvidia because they were captured at different times, so the exact moves should be treated as snapshots. The BBC’s reference to a “bubble” is an ongoing concern voiced by commentators, not a confirmed finding, and the sources do not say whether Anthropic’s shares will recover.
items.op: A strong IPO was supposed to lift the sector, and instead it has become a test of whether investors will keep paying for growth without clear returns. Markets reward transparency about profits, and that discipline should be demanded of every newly listed tech firm asking the public for its money.

items.t: Indian man sentenced to more than 19 years over US plot to kill Sikh separatist in New York
items.s: A federal court in Manhattan has sentenced Nikhil Gupta, an Indian national, to 235 months in prison for plotting to hire a hitman to kill Gurpatwant Singh Pannun. Prosecutors say an Indian government official was involved, a claim New Delhi denies.
p: A Manhattan federal judge imposed the 235-month term on Gupta, 55, according to Al Jazeera, the BBC and the Guardian. He had admitted in February to murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire and conspiracy to commit money laundering.

Prosecutors say Gupta was recruited in May 2023 by Vikash Yadav, whom the BBC describes as an Indian intelligence officer. Yadav allegedly supplied details of Pannun's New York address and daily routine. Court papers indicate that $15,000 in cash was to be handed to a man presented as a hitman, who was in fact an undercover officer.

Gupta was arrested at Prague airport in June 2023 and later extradited to the United States. Al Jazeera reports that his plea agreement called for at least two decades behind bars, while prosecutors had requested about 24 years. The BBC reports the judge said he will likely be deported after serving his sentence.

At the hearing, Gupta apologised and said he had strayed from the nonviolent example of Mahatma Gandhi. “I’m sorry to Mr Pannun, I’m sorry to the communities I hurt, I’m sorry to my own family,” he said.

Yadav is charged in the case but is not in US custody, and it is unclear whether he has a lawyer. India’s government denies any role in the plot and says such conduct would violate its policy. The BBC reports that a spokesperson for the Ministry of External Affairs said Yadav no longer works for the government and that an inquiry committee had been set up to address US security concerns.

Pannun, who attended the hearing, described Gupta as a foot soldier acting on behalf of Prime Minister Narendra Modi, and said the Modi government wanted him dead for leading an open campaign. He said self-determination for Punjab remains his lifetime goal. According to the BBC, India has accused Pannun of terrorism, which he denies.

US and Canadian authorities have linked the case to a wider pattern of alleged plots against Sikh separatists, which has strained relations with New Delhi. The BBC reports that prosecutors allege Gupta called the 2023 killing of Hardeep Singh Nijjar in British Columbia a target as well. India has also denied involvement in that killing.
items.cav: Sources differ on Pannun’s citizenship: Al Jazeera and the Guardian call him a dual US-Canadian citizen, while the BBC calls him American. The allegations against Yadav and Gupta’s remarks about Nijjar are prosecutors’ claims and have not been tested in court here.
items.op: A long sentence for a plot against a critic on American soil is a rightful response. Yet accountability cannot stop at a foot soldier. Washington should press New Delhi to answer the allegations on the record, and openly.

items.t: Trump defends ties with Putin and Xi, accuses Iran of dishonesty in talks
items.s: Back from a four-day tour of Asia, US President Donald Trump used a White House appearance to stand by his dealings with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin. He also pressed Tehran for a “real deal” and set out new trade ideas.
p: Trump said his meetings with both leaders had gone well and described the relationships as a positive sign. He also dismissed people who object to those ties as foolish, a reaction to the criticism that followed his habit of calling Putin a friend. When reporters asked whether Putin counted as a friend of the United States, Trump said he could not answer on behalf of the country. He did, however, describe his own bond with the Russian president in glowing terms.

On Ukraine, Trump claimed that Putin had signalled a preference for ending the fighting through negotiation. He conceded that a settlement had been hard to secure and put much of the blame on the animosity between Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. Asked about guarantees for Kyiv's security, he said Washington was not ready to address that question until a broader agreement was in place.

Separately, the American, Russian and Chinese leaders released a joint declaration in China while the war continues. According to the report, the document commits the three to stability and security at the international level. It also sets out goals for overhauling the United Nations and for limiting the reach of the International Criminal Court.

Turning to Iran, Trump said Tehran wanted a deal with Washington but had not yet put forward terms he could accept. He accused the Iranian government of deceiving its own population for half a century. He further asserted that the US would not tolerate Iran building a so-called dirty bomb, pointing to what he called a rumour. The report stresses that this claim has not been confirmed.

Trump forecast that petrol prices in the US would fall further, though he admitted that the outcome would hinge on how the Iran conflict ends. The report notes that petrol nationwide still costs roughly €0.13 per litre more than when he entered office, which sits awkwardly with his assertion that prices had recently dropped.

On trade, Trump said Washington was nearing an agreement with Mexico after discussions with President Claudia Sheinbaum. He insisted, however, that the US would not accept a surplus running in Mexico's favour. Regarding Canada, he said significant work still lay ahead and accused Ottawa of exploiting American trade for years. He added that Prime Minister Mark Carney was keen to revive the Keystone pipeline, but warned Canada would have to make further concessions first.

Trump also said he planned to levy steep taxes on American firms that build data centres abroad, arguing that such facilities belong at home. He gave no specifics and admitted he had not yet raised the idea with his own advisers. Alongside this, he urged Americans to back data centre projects in their own communities while bargaining for benefits from the developers.
items.cav: All of this comes from one outlet's account of remarks Trump made to reporters, and most of the claims are his own. The dirty bomb assertion is explicitly unconfirmed, and the petrol price claim sits uneasily with the figures the report cites. The data centre tax has no details and no official review, so its scope and timing are unknown.
items.op: Leaders may speak frankly, but treating a war-making president as a friend while floating taxes no adviser has reviewed is a weak basis for policy. Transparency matters most when war and trade are on the table. Voters deserve evidence and considered plans, not rumours and improvised proposals.

items.t: Senate passes fast-track permitting bill that would limit lawsuits and loosen environmental laws
items.s: The US Senate has passed the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, which would speed approval of energy and datacenter projects. Environmental groups oppose it, while some Democrats and the bill’s backers argue it may be the only chance to speed up clean energy.
p: The US Senate has approved a measure that would speed up energy and datacenter construction by loosening some environmental rules and limits on court challenges. The bill, known as the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act or Baaja, still needs to clear the Republican-controlled House before President Donald Trump can sign it, according to the Guardian. Trump has argued that it will raise economic activity and bring down energy costs.

Under the measure, building oil pipelines, power lines, windfarms and datacenters would become considerably simpler. Legal challenges would be curtailed, with lawsuits capped at 150 days. Key environmental statutes, including the Clean Water Act and the Endangered Species Act, would carry less weight when officials decide whether a project may proceed.

Some parts of the bill are presented as safeguards. Large datacenters would be required to cover their own grid and power expenses so that neighbouring communities are not burdened. Transmission line approvals would be sped up through greater coordination among regions, a change that might halve the time needed to build power lines. That provision has drawn praise from Democrats and environmental groups alike.

Future administrations and judges would find it much harder to withdraw or alter permits, including ones that were granted improperly. Businesses, fossil fuel companies among them, could also claim substantial compensation if they can demonstrate that government action delayed them.

Opponents expect the measure to boost fossil fuel activity. Jeff Merkley, a Democrat who is expected to lead the Senate environment committee, warned it would “accelerate the extraction and burning of fossil fuels”. Al Gore described it as a “serious mistake”, and Brett Hartl of the Center for Biological Diversity called it “the largest giveaway in history” to polluters.

Backers, including Democratic senator Sheldon Whitehouse, who co-sponsored the bill, contend that it may be the best opening to move forward on renewable projects now stuck in regulatory backlogs. Whitehouse said Democrats could not afford to hold out for an “imaginary perfect bill” once they regain control of Congress in January. Fellow Democrat Martin Heinrich, who co-wrote the bill, said voters need relief now. The bill was co-authored with Republicans Shelley Moore Capito and Mike Lee.

The Guardian reports that roughly 85% of generation awaiting grid connection in the US is solar, wind or battery storage. Citing the Rhodium Group, it says the bill could cut up to 1.5bn tons of pollution by 2040 and lower household electricity bills by as much as $78 a year by the same date. Merkley dismissed those savings as a “mere $5 a month” in 15 years. The bill was voted on without any hearings, and tribal groups say they were not consulted.
items.cav: The emissions and savings figures come from a Rhodium Group analysis cited by the Guardian, and critics dispute how meagre they are. The article does not say whether the House will pass the bill, and it is unclear how much Republican support a stronger bill written in January would receive. Klein’s concerns about vague provisions are reported second-hand.
items.op: Speed is worth having, but not at the cost of a law written behind closed doors while tribal consultation is brushed aside. Permits that courts and future governments cannot revisit is a transparency problem as much as an environmental one. Lawmakers should slow down enough to write these rules in public.

items.t: EU and UK agree post-Brexit reset as Russian missiles hit Poland, COP31 talks stall
items.s: EU and UK leaders reached a post-Brexit reset at a Brussels summit, according to Euronews. The same broadcast also flagged Russian projectiles landing in Poland and stalled climate talks in Antalya.
p: At the Brussels summit, leaders from both sides settled on looser trade rules for farm goods, closer alignment of their carbon pricing systems and a scheme that would let young people move between the two. They also committed to further talks on how the relationship should develop. Prime Minister Andy Burnham was reported to hint at a tighter arrangement after the next election.

Euronews reports that two Russian missiles came down in southeastern Poland during lethal overnight strikes on Ukraine. Warsaw has described the landing as a deliberate provocation. The incident followed a joint pledge by Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin to work toward global peace. The broadcast also cites reports that Washington is weighing NATO membership for Ukraine if Kyiv gave up the Donbas region.

In Antalya, negotiators at the COP31 climate summit missed their scheduled close and extended talks into the weekend. Four disputes remain open: a timetable for moving away from fossil fuels, whether a 2035 electrification target of 35% depends on clean power, how climate finance will be delivered, and how to make the energy shift fair for every worker and community.
items.cav: This is a programme preview built on a broadcast summary, not a full report, so the terms of the EU-UK deal and the circumstances of the missile incident are not set out. The NATO proposal is described only as reported, and no outcome for the COP31 talks is yet known.
items.op: Trade terms and security claims should be judged on published texts, not on a teaser. If Warsaw’s charge of deliberate provocation is made, and talk of Ukraine ceding Donbas is real, citizens are owed open evidence and open debate.

items.t: Itoje rules out win-at-all-costs approach as England prepare to face All Blacks at Twickenham
items.s: England captain Maro Itoje has said he will never adopt a win-at-all-costs mentality, ahead of Saturday’s match against the All Blacks at Twickenham. He also called for respect for referees after South Africa’s Rassie Erasmus was sanctioned over his match-fixing remarks.
p: England captain Maro Itoje has said he will never adopt a win-at-all-costs mentality as his side prepare to face the All Blacks at Twickenham on Saturday. The Guardian reports that Itoje spoke after a week in sport dominated by comments from Springboks head coach Rassie Erasmus and the resurfacing of the 2018 sandpaper affair involving the Australia cricket team.

Itoje said England could take a significant step by winning back-to-back matches against New Zealand, something not achieved since 2003. He said his Christian faith and sense of right and wrong shape the limits he sets for himself. “There’s a line,” he said, adding that he would not take part in performance-enhancing drugs or betting on a game, even to win.

The context is Erasmus’s recent ban. According to the report, he was suspended for six matches after suggesting that officials might be match-fixing and that they had “manipulated the game”. The comments were widely seen as an attempt to put pressure on match officials before the Springboks’ upcoming fixtures.

Itoje backed the position taken by England head coach Steve Borthwick and several other coaches around the world that referees must be protected. Like Borthwick, he did not directly address Erasmus. He pointed out that World Rugby had acted against the coach and said players should uphold the values they want the sport to keep after they leave the field.

Itoje also said referees face heavy criticism, particularly online, and that rugby is praised by people in other sports, especially football, for the respect it shows officials. He noted that New Zealand and England supporters will sit side by side at Twickenham and said mutual respect is a value the rugby community should hold on to.

England arrive on the back of four consecutive wins and still have a chance of reaching next week’s Nations Championship final. Next year’s World Cup is also looming. Itoje said the coming games were the kind England must play if they want to become a great side, because they will face highly motivated and strong opponents.
items.cav: The report relies on Itoje’s own comments and on the Guardian’s description of Erasmus’s remarks as a cynical attempt to pressure officials; the article does not give Erasmus’s full statement or his response. Itoje’s quotation refers to Erasmus being banned three times, while the same report says he was banned for six matches, and the sources do not reconcile the two.
items.op: Itoje is right that referees deserve protection, because rules only work when those who enforce them are trusted. Claims of match-fixing made without evidence erode that trust, whoever makes them. Sport should answer such accusations with transparent process and clear sanctions, not with rhetoric.

items.t: Africa’s negotiators say rich nations are undermining COP31 as talks near their deadline
items.s: African ministers accused rich countries of breaking Paris commitments as the Antalya climate summit entered its final official day. Disputes over finance threaten to push the talks past their scheduled end.
p: African ministers said on Friday that rich countries were undermining the process, trust and credibility of the UN climate summit by failing to meet their commitments under the Paris agreement. The remarks came on the last official day of the Cop31 talks in Antalya, Turkey.

Zanetor Agyeman-Rawlings, chair of the African Group of Negotiators, told a press conference: “We didn’t come here to beg.” She said African countries were being excluded through technical rules, finance that was hard to access, and targets that kept shifting.

Agyeman-Rawlings said the draft texts on climate finance, a just transition mechanism and a global goal on adaptation did not yet make sense to people in Africa. She added that Africa was “not a continent merely seeking assistance” and was asking developed countries to keep promises they had already made.

Civil society groups had earlier named the EU as leading a bloc of rich countries that was obstructing progress on finance, the just transition and adaptation. Al Jazeera, in a separate report, said Ghana had demanded climate justice and funding for African nations and warned leaders against empty promises. That report’s details were not available beyond a short summary.

The EU rejected the criticism. A senior EU official said the bloc provided the largest share of global climate finance, citing €32.3bn from public sources and €9.3bn mobilised from private finance in 2025. Another EU official said the current draft decision was “unbalanced” and warned of a possible no-deal outcome unless there was substantial movement.

Cop negotiations president Chris Bowen said there was still a spirit of goodwill after overnight talks with blocs and with his Turkish counterpart, Murat Kurum. He also responded to an open letter from Panama that set out demands in return for its support of any agreement.

Separately, the US held its first deep-sea mining lease sales off American Samoa on Thursday, despite an adverse court ruling earlier in the week and local opposition, according to reporting by the Guardian. Two areas covering parts of a 12.7m hectare seabed zone were sold for $3m each to Wetstone US Ventures, the only bidder, according to a spokesperson for the Marine Minerals Administration. The buyer gains permission for preliminary surveys, not full mining.

Interior secretary Doug Burgum called the sale a historic step for America’s energy and mineral security. Critics and local groups have raised concerns, and the Guardian’s report did not detail the full terms of the court ruling.
items.cav: The sources do not say whether the summit will overrun its official end, and the Al Jazeera account is available only as a short summary. The EU’s figures and its characterisation of the draft text come from anonymous officials and have not been independently verified.
items.op: Climate finance promises only mean something if they are measured and delivered. Rich countries that signed the Paris agreement should publish clear, checkable figures and explain delays in plain terms. Without that transparency, the trust that the process depends on will keep eroding.

items.t: Polish officials say Russian cruise missile crashed in Poland during Western military drill
items.s: Polish authorities say a Russian cruise missile was one of three objects that entered the country’s airspace early on Friday. Prime Minister Donald Tusk said the timing did not look accidental.
p: Early on Friday, Polish authorities reported that three objects had breached the country’s airspace, one of them a Russian cruise missile. Officials said no one had been injured and that no damage had been reported so far. According to Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz, the Kh-101 missile struck open countryside at Nowy Lipowiec in the southeast, roughly 50km (31 miles) from the Ukrainian frontier, at about 06:30 local time.

A local resident, Natalie Szponar, was quoted as saying she was getting her children ready for school when she heard a whistling sound followed by a muffled thud. Footage from a farm camera captured the impact. Officials later said residents faced no danger.

Kosiniak-Kamysz added that another suspected missile came down near Rudnik nad Sanem, west of the impact site, and that a jet-powered drone fell to the south, near Mołodycz. He described the incursion as a “provocation” by Russia and said Warsaw would seek additional support from Nato.

Tusk told reporters the objects landed close to Nowa Dęba, where a military exercise supported by Polish troops was under way, and said that was “no coincidence”. Moscow has not commented on the violations, which coincided with one of the largest aerial attacks on Ukraine since the full-scale invasion began in 2022.

Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte condemned the breaches as serious and said alliance jets had been scrambled in response. He said the episode was clearly dangerous and stemmed from Russia’s war on Ukraine. Rutte is due to travel to Warsaw on Saturday. UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham called the incident intolerable, while UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting, visiting Poland, said the fallout of the war was spreading into neighbouring countries. European Council President António Costa voiced support for the Polish people and urged Russia to enter negotiations.

The exercise, named Koalicja 2026, is led by Britain and France and includes 11 countries from the Coalition of the Willing, a Western grouping preparing for a possible peace deal in Ukraine. The violations came a day after a Berlin summit attended by 40 countries, where Chancellor Friedrich Merz argued that talks with Russia should begin soon on neutral ground. The same day, at least eight people were killed when Russian missiles and drones hit three bridges over the Dnipro in Kyiv and a station in Lviv. Days earlier, Vladimir Putin had promised a painful response to repeated strikes on the Kerch Strait bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea.

Spillover into Poland is not new. In July, a cruise missile landed in the country during an attack on Lviv, leaving a crater 10m (33ft) wide. Casualties in Poland have been rare, although two Polish farmers were killed by a missile in November 2022, which was believed to be a Ukrainian air-defence missile fired at a Russian attack. On Friday, Moldovan officials said a drone briefly entered their airspace during Russian strikes on Ukraine, and that the country’s defence ministry has recorded 118 such violations since February 2022.
items.cav: Russia has not responded, so the account of the missile’s origin rests on Polish officials and their allies. The second missile and the drone are described as suspected, and the 2022 attribution is only a belief, not a confirmed finding.
items.op: Every breach of a Nato member’s airspace should be met with a clear public account of what crossed the border and who sent it. Poland and its allies are entitled to verifiable facts, not only ministers’ assessments. Moscow, which has offered no comment, should be pressed to explain itself.

items.t: White House national cyber director ousted amid a wave of US tech outages
items.s: Sean Cairncross, the White House national cyber director, has reportedly been fired days after outages hit US air travel, banking and national security networks. The White House has not officially confirmed the move or given a reason.
p: Several outlets report that Sean Cairncross has left his post as the White House national cyber director, the top cyber-security role in the US government. The reports rely on unnamed sources, and the timing follows a run of technology failures across the country.

According to CBS, which the BBC cites as its US news partner, Cairncross lost the confidence of White House chief of staff Stephen Miller. Reuters, citing a person close to the White House who spoke on condition of anonymity, said the president fully supported the firing. AFP and CBS also reported that sources said President Donald Trump backed the decision.

Axios was the first to report the departure. It cited anonymous officials who said Miller pushed for the change because Cairncross “lacked the strong cyber credentials to perform the job”. That explanation has not been confirmed on the record.
There has been no official confirmation of the removal, and the White House has not publicly explained why Cairncross left. The BBC has asked the White House for comment.

Kirsten Davies, the Pentagon’s chief information officer, is expected to take over on a temporary or acting basis, according to the sources and White House officials cited by the reports. Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced on X that he looked forward to working with her. Davies thanked Trump and Miller on X for their confidence, and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth praised her as a dedicated professional.

The outages affected a nationwide halt to air travel, a Microsoft email disruption, banking and e-commerce services, and a temporary problem on a National Security Agency internal network. US officials said the failures were not caused by cyberattacks. The top US intelligence official said on Wednesday they were separate outages linked to maintenance and technical changes. Rubio said there was “zero evidence” the outages were connected. Some members of Congress have demanded a clearer account of what went wrong.

Cairncross, a former Republican Party lawyer, served as chief operating officer of the Republican National Committee and was part of the White House chief of staff’s team in Trump’s first term. He later worked in the private sector and returned to government in August 2025. Trump nominated him for the cyber post in 2025, and the Senate confirmed him. The office advises the president on cyber policy, coordinates policy across federal agencies and was first set up in 2021.

Any permanent successor will need Senate confirmation. The Guardian reports that the Senate will be controlled by Democrats from January. Some people have also voiced worry about the safety of the technology that daily life relies on heavily, given how many failures have come in quick succession.
items.cav: The removal is not officially confirmed, and the reasons for it come from anonymous sources, including Axios’s account of Miller’s objections. The sources also differ on how definitive the outage explanation is: officials say there was no cyberattack, but Congress has asked for more detail.
items.op: A top cyber post should not change hands in a fog of anonymous briefings. If the outages were routine maintenance failures, the public deserves a clear account of what broke, why, and who answers for it. Silence on the reasons for a firing only deepens suspicion. Transparency is cheap, and it is the only way to restore trust.

items.t: Downing Street says UK-EU reset is agreed, but EU student fees remain open
items.s: No 10 says London and Brussels have concluded a reset agreement, yet the fees that EU students will pay at British universities are still undecided. EU sources argue that three of the accords will not take effect without a fees settlement.
p: Downing Street announced that negotiations on a reset between the UK and the European Union have concluded, while the fee rate for European students at British universities has not been set. A No 10 statement declared the agreement finished shortly after Prime Minister Andy Burnham reached the Brussels summit venue. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa were there to receive him.

According to the statement, three arrangements are now settled: food and drink, emissions trading, and a youth mobility scheme. EU sources, however, say those arrangements will not come into force unless London reaches a separate settlement with the bloc on fees for European students. Friday’s reports had already warned that the fee question might drag down other parts of the process.

British officials rejected that linkage. They maintained that the fees question and the three arrangements are unrelated. In their account, the new food and agriculture rules will apply from March 2028 whether or not fees are resolved, and fee talks have a further six months to run. Officials also said the UK had obtained agreement that it could potentially join the EU’s still-unfinished “Made in Europe” initiative, which is designed to curb Chinese influence over European industry. One official described this as a significant gain.

The dispute over fees comes down to the rate. Brussels wants EU students charged the domestic rate, currently capped at £9,790 for this academic year, rather than the international rate, which can be four or five times higher. On Thursday night the EU accepted a six-month delay on a fees deal but says it will keep pushing for domestic rates. Two EU sources told the Guardian that, in last-minute talks, the UK floated a figure as low as £12,000. Those figures come from the EU side and have not been confirmed by the UK government.

A statement from the main EU institutions, which the Guardian has seen, ties the fees question directly to the package. It says equal treatment with nationals on tuition fees is required and describes the four agreements as one bundle. An EU official said Brussels’ stance had been consistent and that the matter must be dealt with.

The two sides also agreed a youth mobility scheme allowing 100,000 young people from each side to live, work, travel and study across the Channel for up to three years. Speaking to business leaders, Burnham argued that closer ties were the sensible course and called the day a potentially positive one for the country.

Opposition has already emerged in Britain. Nigel Farage, leader of Reform UK, who was also in Brussels, told LBC radio that the deal would tie Britain to part of the EU single market and make it a rule-taker. He described the move as unnecessary and said European officials were steering the prime minister. These are Farage’s own claims and the sources do not test them.
items.cav: The fee rate is unresolved, and the £12,000 figure rests on two unnamed EU sources that the UK has not confirmed. London and Brussels disagree on whether the three agreements depend on the fees settlement. Farage’s criticism is opinion, not established fact.
items.op: A deal whose fate hinges on what students pay should be explained in full. Families and universities on both sides of the Channel need to see the fee figures and who would bear them. Until those terms are public, the reset is a headline, not a settled agreement.

items.t: ICJ rules Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya, and the Gaza case looms large
items.s: The International Court of Justice has found that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority, according to Al Jazeera, which calls it the court’s first genocide verdict since its founding in 1945. Observers say the ruling could shape how the court approaches South Africa’s pending case against Israel.
p: On Thursday, the United Nations’ top court in The Hague ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya, a majority-Muslim minority. Al Jazeera describes the decision as historic and the first genocide verdict the court has issued since it was established in 1945.

About 1.2 million Rohingya are living in crowded refugee camps in Bangladesh, and more than 500,000 remain in Myanmar, where Al Jazeera says they are still targeted. The article links the case to decades of persecution, torture and killings by the Myanmar military and non-Rohingya rebel groups in Rakhine state. The Gambia first accused Myanmar of genocide in November 2019.

Nine of the court’s 15 judges concluded that the only reasonable inference from the evidence was that genocide had occurred. The court said Myanmar knowingly allowed civilian militias to take part in targeting the Rohingya, failed to investigate or punish culpable commanders, acted with intent to destroy the group, and breached provisional measures issued in 2020 to preserve evidence.

ICJ President Yuji Iwasawa said Myanmar’s security forces had killed thousands of Rohingya civilians, carried out widespread sexual violence and attacked people fleeing to Bangladesh. The court ordered reparations, including the safe return of Rohingya to their lands, compensation, replacing damaged property, accounting for missing people, reuniting families, dignified burials, medical and trauma care, and guarantees that such violations will not recur.

Al Jazeera reports that experts see strong implications for South Africa’s case against Israel over the war in Gaza. South Africa filed its application on December 29, 2023. Palestinian political analyst Ahmed Najar told Al Jazeera that “This judgement will not decide the Gaza case,” but may shape the legal lens through which Gaza is eventually judged.

The article notes that the ICJ has already issued several orders in the Gaza matter, including emergency measures in January 2024, a food-access order in March 2024 and an order in May 2024 to halt the Rafah ground invasion. Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International have concluded that Israel did not comply with these orders. Israel has argued that it acted in self-defence after the Hamas-led attacks of October 7, 2023.

Al Jazeera puts the death toll in Gaza at close to 75,000, and says a verdict on genocide there is not expected for several years, with South Africa’s next submission due in November 2027. For both the Rohingya and Palestinians, the article says, legal proceedings have brought little immediate relief, and civilians are still being killed.
items.cav: The Gaza analysis comes from Al Jazeera and the experts it quotes, not from the court, which has not ruled on genocide in Gaza. Compliance claims and casualty figures are attributed to Al Jazeera, Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International, and the evidence does not include Israel’s or Myanmar’s response to the verdict beyond Israel’s earlier self-defence argument.
items.op: A genocide finding matters only if it is enforced. The court has ordered Myanmar to make reparations, and its credibility will depend on applying the same rigour to Gaza, where earlier orders were reportedly ignored. Evidence should be judged on its substance, not on whether a formal order was signed.

items.t: Schneier Blames Economic Incentives, Not Cyber-Attacks, for Recent Tech Outages
items.s: Security technologist Bruce Schneier argues that a run of outages at major firms and agencies should not be blamed on coordinated cyber-attacks. He places the root cause in the economic incentives that shape how technology is built and maintained.
p: In a column published on 20 November 2026 in the Guardian, security technologist Bruce Schneier argues that a recent cluster of technology failures should not be put down to cyber-attacks. He says the underlying problem is economic, not technical.

Schneier lists outages at Microsoft, the FAA, a handful of banks, United Airlines, an unnamed classified NSA network, and Apple. He acknowledges that people may suspect a coordinated attack, a common cause or a conspiracy, but he writes that there is none. In his view the incidents are unrelated and were not the result of any cyber-attack.
He is more cautious about the NSA case. Schneier says he cannot comment on it and that the details will probably never become public.

He describes much of the underlying infrastructure as old, patched and upgraded piece by piece over decades. According to him, a surprising amount is maintained by hobbyists who are not paid, backup systems are often weak, and more systems are centralised, so one failure can spread across many areas of life. He concludes that a lot of this technology only just works.

The root cause, he argues, lies in how these systems are funded. Security, resilience and recoverability cost money without producing near-term profit. Schneier blames shareholder capitalism and private equity for prioritising quick returns, and says monopolisation removes the competitive pressure that would otherwise push firms to improve their services.

Companies can also pass the cost of failure on to the public, he writes. Travellers are left stranded when planes do not fly, and customers struggle when they cannot withdraw money. In his account, such brittle systems, with single points of failure, are more exposed both to attacks and to ordinary mistakes.

His proposed remedy is regulation with real enforcement and meaningful fines, alongside strict antitrust action. He concedes this is hard to achieve, especially in the US, where he says monied interests have a tight hold on the legislative agenda. Until that changes, he expects more failures of this kind.
items.cav: This is an opinion column, and Schneier’s explanation for the individual outages is his own assessment rather than established fact. The source does not give technical root causes for each incident, and he says the NSA case is one we will probably never fully understand.
items.op: When banks, airlines and public bodies fail together, ordinary people absorb the damage for decisions made in boardrooms. Governments should stop treating resilience as an optional expense and write enforceable rules with penalties that genuinely bite. Companies that profit from fragile systems should carry the cost of their own failures.

items.t: BepiColombo nears Mercury after an eight-year voyage to study the planet closest to the Sun
items.s: The European-Japanese BepiColombo spacecraft is about to enter orbit around Mercury after a journey of almost six billion miles, according to BBC News. The mission aims to deliver the best view yet of a planet that has been little explored.
p: After an eight-year journey covering almost six billion miles (10bn km), the BepiColombo spacecraft is about to reach Mercury and go into orbit around the planet, BBC News reports. The mission is a collaboration between the European Space Agency (ESA) and Japan’s space agency, JAXA, and it is expected to give scientists their best view of Mercury so far.

The environment is harsh. Temperatures on Mercury can reach 430C and then plunge to -180C, and the planet is constantly hit by intense solar radiation. The spacecraft lifted off from French Guiana in 2018. Because the Sun’s gravity is so strong this close in, it has kept its brakes on for the whole trip, following a winding route that looped once around Earth, twice around Venus and six times around Mercury.

The journey was meant to take seven years, but a problem with the propulsion system added a year. The final manoeuvre is the most perilous part: a 37-minute “handbrake turn” that allows the planet’s gravity to capture the craft.

Scientists hope the mission will solve several puzzles. One is why ice survives in Mercury’s craters despite its proximity to the Sun. Another is the thousands of shallow hollows scattered across the surface. They have steep sides, often cluster together and are described as young, at about 100,000 years old. Researchers know they are not impact craters, but they are not sure how they formed.

Mercury also has a huge metal core for such a small world, roughly only a bit bigger than the Moon. Prof Emma Bunce of Leicester University, a principal investigator on the mission, said the planet could once have been much larger and may have been the victim of a “hit and run” early in its history. One explanation is that its mantle was stripped away in a large collision. Another is that it formed that way in a metal-rich part of the early Solar System. Bunce also described Mercury as an “under-loved planet”.

The mission carries two spacecraft. The ESA craft will study the surface up close, while the JAXA craft will observe the planet from a distance. Jessica Marshall, a systems engineer at Airbus, who helped build the spacecraft, said the moment of separation would be “nerve-wracking” for the team.
items.cav: The evidence is a preview written before the orbit insertion, so it does not confirm whether the manoeuvre succeeded. The 100,000-year age of the hollows and the explanations for Mercury’s core are presented as scientific possibilities rather than settled findings.
items.op: Large public science missions deserve candid reporting on delays, risks and costs, not only triumphant previews. BepiColombo’s seven-year plan became eight, and its most dangerous step still lies ahead. Agencies should publish setbacks as readily as they publish spacecraft selfies.

items.t: Anthropic closes first day of trading about 17% above IPO price after record $81.3bn listing
items.s: Anthropic, the startup behind the Claude chatbot, ended its first day of US trading about 17% above its offer price. The Guardian reported that the listing raised $81.3bn, surpassing the previous record set by SpaceX.
p: Anthropic’s shares closed at just over $97 on Thursday, according to the Guardian, compared with an initial public offering price of $83. The stock had reached an early high of $111.50 and rose 34% when trading opened, a move that briefly valued the company at more than $2tn.

At the close, the company had a total market capitalisation of nearly $1.3tn, or $1.75tn on a fully diluted basis. The Guardian reported that Anthropic’s chief executive, Dario Amodei, rang the Nasdaq opening bell.

Anthropic announced late on Wednesday that it had sold 980m shares to underwriters in an upsized offering. The Guardian said the deal raised $81.3bn, beating SpaceX’s initial $75bn fundraise in June, and described the listing as one of the biggest stock market flotations in history.

The broader market was less enthusiastic. US stocks slumped at the end of trading, and most major chipmakers closed lower than they opened. Nvidia extended its losses to a sixth day after its latest earnings call, while Micron and Broadcom also saw their shares decline.

Analysts at Yorkville Ives said Anthropic is the first firm focused entirely on its field to be publicly traded, and wrote that the listing could help restore investor confidence. Evan Schlossman, a principal at Neostellar, said investors will focus on whether the company’s growth rate can be sustained once it is public.

According to its investor prospectus, filed at the end of October, Anthropic brought in $16.2bn in revenue in the first six months of 2026, up from $4.6bn for all of 2025. The company also reported losses of $80bn in the first half, which it said were largely due to a one-off charge, and losses of $104bn over the first nine months.

Computing power, supplied by arrays of semiconductor chips often housed in datacenters, was Anthropic’s largest single expense, at about $18.8bn in the first nine months of 2026. The executives wrote in the prospectus that they expect costs to balloon as the company secures more of it.

The Guardian also noted that Anthropic has detailed in its filings how its technology could pose dangers, including being used to develop bioweapons, and that Amodei has called for a slowdown in the development of the most advanced systems. The listing comes as the industry braces for possible fallout from a recent Nvidia scandal that led to the resignation of its chief executive, Jensen Huang.
items.cav: This account rests on a single outlet, and the revenue and loss figures are taken from the company’s prospectus as reported, not from independent verification. The Nvidia scandal and Huang’s resignation are mentioned only in passing, without detail on what happened.
items.op: A public listing is only as credible as the disclosures behind it. Investors can now weigh Anthropic’s $104bn in losses against its revenue, and that scrutiny is exactly what transparency should invite. Regulators and reporters should keep demanding audited, consistent figures rather than accepting the upbeat headline.

items.t: European leaders say they are ready for talks with Russia to end the war in Ukraine
items.s: At a Berlin summit of Ukraine’s allies, European leaders said they were ready to negotiate with Russia, but Moscow has given mixed signals on whether Europe will get a seat at the table.
p: European leaders said at a summit in Berlin that they were ready for negotiations with Russia to end the war in Ukraine, in a show of support for Kyiv. The gathering of Ukraine’s allies, known as the Coalition of the Willing, was reported by the BBC.

According to the BBC, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Europe had a “clear and consistent and united negotiating position.” German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said Moscow’s maximalist demands were not realistic, and that serious talks with Russia on European security should be matched by a peace agreement with Ukraine first.

The summit followed historic trilateral talks in Shenzhen, in south-eastern China, between Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping. Trump joined the Berlin summit by phone from Air Force One, the report said.

Jared Kushner, one of two US envoys in Berlin, said Trump had come away from Shenzhen believing that peace was achievable. He said the Russians were willing for Europeans to be at the table, and that Moscow was “comfortable” with Ukraine receiving security guarantees modelled on Nato’s Article Five.

Putin said at a press conference after the talks that Russia was not against European participation but wanted to know what Europe would bring. He said Moscow had invited Europeans to Moscow to clarify their positions. He also said Russia was not planning to attack anyone, and questioned talk in Europe of war coming in 2030.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron were less optimistic. Zelensky said Putin had always said no to proposals so far. Macron urged allies to do the maximum to deliver air defence systems to Kyiv and called for the question of Ukraine’s Nato membership to be reopened. Reports say US negotiators have considered Article Five-style guarantees for Ukraine without Nato membership, if Kyiv agreed to painful territorial concessions.

The Russian position remains unclear. US envoys Steve Witkoff and Kushner had appeared certain after a Moscow visit that Europe would soon have a seat, but Putin’s aide Yury Ushakov said a great deal would have to be done before the format could expand.

On the same day, drones struck several buildings in Kyiv’s historic centre. One person was killed in a strike on a residential building in the Podilskyi neighbourhood, and the Dutch and Austrian embassies and Saint Volodymyr’s Cathedral reported damage. Putin vowed that Moscow’s response to a Ukrainian strike on the Crimean Bridge would be “considerably more painful,” and said he had discussed a possible ceasefire but decided against it after that attack.
items.cav: Putin’s claims and the US envoys’ upbeat assessments are the statements of the parties themselves and are not independently confirmed. Reports about possible guarantees without Nato membership are second-hand, and the sources do not say what happened in the Crimean Bridge attack or who carried it out.
items.op: Peace talks cannot be built on understandings struck between great powers while the country under attack is kept at the edge of the room. Any settlement that trades Ukrainian territory or security without Kyiv’s full consent would reward the party that rejected every offer so far. Governments should publish what is being discussed in Shenzhen and Berlin.

items.t: UN top court finds Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya in 2017 crackdown
items.s: The International Court of Justice has ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority, the first time the court has held a state responsible for the crime. The finding concerns a 2017 military crackdown in Rakhine State.
p: The UN’s highest court, the International Court of Justice (ICJ), has concluded that Myanmar carried out genocide against the Rohingya, according to the BBC and a French broadcaster. Both reports describe the Thursday decision as unprecedented, since no international court had previously held a state responsible for genocide in this way.

ICJ president Yuji Iwasawa said Myanmar acted with an “intention to destroy” a large part of the Rohingya population and destroyed evidence on a wide scale to conceal its conduct. As the BBC relayed his remarks, he described indiscriminate killings, executions of men, widespread sexual violence, severe violence against children and the deliberate burning of Rohingya homes, as well as attacks on people fleeing to Bangladesh.

The judgement was reached by a majority of nine votes to six. The court also found that Myanmar had breached several other provisions of the 1948 Genocide Convention. The French broadcaster said the panel of 15 judges had spent seven years weighing the case, which The Gambia brought against Myanmar.

The reports give different figures for the scale of the violence. The BBC said the ICJ determined that around 10,000 Rohingya were killed during the operation and that about 815,000 had been targeted in some way, with more than 700,000 thought to have fled to Bangladesh. The French report spoke of thousands of killings and said at least 700,000 people were driven out of Myanmar.

Myanmar has rejected the genocide claims throughout, saying its operations targeted militant threats after attacks by the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army. Its representative, Ko Ko Hlaing, told the court in January that the state could not stand by while “terrorists” roamed freely. After the ruling he declined to comment, the BBC reported.

The French report noted that Min Aung Hlaing, who commanded the military during the crackdown, later ousted the elected government in a 2021 coup. This year he was installed as civilian president after heavily restricted elections. The ICJ has no means of enforcing its rulings, but the finding is likely to add diplomatic pressure on him.

According to the BBC, the court said Myanmar must pay proportionate reparations, though the exact amount could be set later. Rohingya communities and human rights groups welcomed the decision. UN human rights chief Volker Türk described the suffering of the Rohingya as a stain on humanity’s conscience and urged that the ruling lead to concrete action.

Mohammed Nowkim, a Rohingya who fled Rakhine in 2017 and now lives in Canada, told the BBC that the verdict amounted to a formal acknowledgment of what his community endured. Legal observers will also watch a separate ICJ case, brought by South Africa, which accuses Israel of genocide against Palestinians in Gaza, for signs of how the court approaches such claims.
items.cav: The reports give different casualty and displacement figures, with the BBC citing about 10,000 killed and the French report citing thousands, so the precise toll is not settled by these sources. Survivor accounts are reported as testimony and have not been independently verified here.
items.op: The verdict matters because it tests whether the Genocide Convention means anything when the state itself is accused. Recognition alone is not justice: reparations, prosecutions and open access to evidence must follow, or the ruling will remain words on paper.

items.t: European leaders reject ‘Yalta 2.0’ for Ukraine after Trump, Putin and Xi talks
items.s: European leaders have rejected any attempt to repeat the 1945 Yalta Conference over Ukraine, a day after Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping met in China. Berlin hosted a parallel gathering of Kyiv’s backers.
p: Continental leaders are pushing back against any effort to revive the logic of the 1945 Yalta Conference as a way to end Russia’s war, according to Euronews. The concern is that such an arrangement would carve Europe into zones of influence.

The objection surfaced on Thursday at a session of the Coalition of the Willing, a grouping of Kyiv’s allies, convened in Berlin by Chancellor Friedrich Merz. It followed by only a few hours a trilateral encounter in Shenzhen between Putin, Trump and Xi, which commentators have labelled “Yalta 2.0”.
Although the three leaders discussed Ukraine, the joint text they issued, called “Declaration Toward Peace”, made no reference to the country, the report said.

Merz argued that a Yalta-style arrangement would not produce peace, and pledged that Europe would not accept a repeat of such a division. French President Emmanuel Macron said the Shenzhen statement, which contained four points, did not mirror the 1945 outcome that preceded the Cold War. He insisted that any negotiation must bring Ukraine, Europe, the United States and Russia to the same table.

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham supported that stance, holding that Ukraine cannot be decided on without Ukraine present. Volodymyr Zelenskyy, the Ukrainian president, read the Berlin meeting as evidence that Moscow had not managed to split European allies.

According to the report, the four leaders agreed that Europe should now hold direct talks with Russia, a step not yet taken. Europe has named a joint team of seven envoys, drawn from France, Britain, Germany, Poland, Italy, the EU institutions and NATO, for the next round. US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, who travelled to Berlin, also urged Russia to accept European participation.

Putin, speaking in Shenzhen, said he had proposed through diplomatic channels that Europeans travel to Moscow to set out their positions, after which the Kremlin would decide whether to continue dialogue with Kyiv. He also questioned discussing Europe’s security without Europe. Macron described Moscow’s demands on the continent’s security structure as excessive.

Merz said that debate on European security would only follow a settled peace in Ukraine. Guarantees under discussion include a clause modelled on NATO’s collective defence provision in case Russia attacks again, and a European-led peacekeeping force, which Putin has said he would reject in any case. Kushner called an Article 5-style guarantee a significant step that Trump might accept if it served American interests.

Kushner confirmed that Trump joined the closed-door Berlin discussions by phone from his aircraft. Media reports suggest Trump voiced doubts about Europe’s military support for Ukraine, yet the leaders present seemed unmoved and agreed that assistance would continue.
items.cav: The account rests on a single outlet’s reporting. Trump’s scepticism about European military support comes from unnamed media reports, and the guarantees and peacekeeping force remain under discussion without final terms.
items.op: Europe is right to insist that decisions on its security are made with Europe and Ukraine at the table. A joint statement that does not even name Ukraine is a poor basis for peace, and deals made over the heads of the affected countries should never be presented as settlements. Transparent, rule-based talks are the only durable route.

items.t: Trump leaves China without meeting Kim Jong-un as three-way summit raises concerns across Asia
items.s: US President Donald Trump departed China without the Kim Jong-un encounter he had sought, while a rare summit with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin left South Korea, Japan and Taiwan uneasy about being sidelined.
p: Trump flew out of Shenzhen on Thursday with no meeting held with the North Korean leader, despite having pursued one during the trip. The stop was built around a seldom-seen gathering of Trump, Xi and Putin on the fringes of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit.

Trump had raised the idea of a Kim meeting many times, though a White House official had said none was scheduled. On Monday he told reporters at the White House that a encounter with Kim might still happen, calling that prospect welcome.
Kim, for his part, was reported by the South Korean agency Newsis to have toured locations in North Korea’s South Hamgyong province on Tuesday and Wednesday.

The three leaders committed to continuing talks on reducing nuclear risks and curbing proliferation. Their joint declaration, however, never named the Korean Peninsula or Taiwan. Xinhua, China’s state news agency, later indicated that the leaders had compared notes on the peninsula, Ukraine, nuclear non-proliferation and the Middle East.

Concern in South Korea, Japan and Taiwan centres on the worry that big powers might settle matters touching their security without involving them. Seoul’s media drew comparisons with the 1945 Yalta Conference. Money Today, a South Korean outlet, argued that leaving the peninsula out eased fears of a repeat but suggested denuclearisation is losing ground on the diplomatic agenda. Park Won-gon of Ewha Womans University thought China and Russia might have taken Pyongyang’s side, while Kim Jae-chun of Sogang University saw the three powers as far apart on North Korea’s nuclear programme. Newsis argued that the lack of a Trump-Kim meeting for a second year could reduce worries about Washington recognising North Korea as a nuclear-armed state. President Lee Jae-myung, speaking at APEC, again stressed peace and stability on the peninsula.

Japan’s Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi greeted Xi at APEC, but the two held no formal talks. A ruling-party lawmaker told Fuji TV that Japan’s exclusion could look like a diplomatic setback. Takaichi told reporters in Shenzhen she did not think Japan’s interests would suffer, according to TBS. Citing government sources, TV Asahi reported she is setting up a call with Trump.

The declaration also asked for respect for the immunity of state officials and warned that the International Criminal Court and similar bodies must not overreach. The court is currently led by Japanese judge Tomoko Akane. It issued an arrest warrant for Putin in March 2023 over the alleged unlawful deportation of Ukrainian children. Japanese media drew attention to this passage.

In Taiwan, TVBS warned the island could become a bargaining chip. Taiwan came up in the Xi-Trump talks earlier on Thursday. Tsai Jung-hsiang of National Chung Cheng University told the Central News Agency that Washington and Beijing read strategic stability very differently, and that Xi wants Washington to accept Beijing’s claim over sovereignty. Tsai said he expects no shift in US Taiwan policy from the meeting.
Chinese state media presented the three-way meeting as a chance for the major powers to cooperate on international security and stability.
items.cav: The sources disagree on whether the Korean Peninsula was discussed: the joint declaration does not mention it, while Xinhua says the leaders exchanged views on it. Kim’s activities, Trump’s plans and Takaichi’s planned call rest on Newsis, the White House and Japanese government sources reported by others. Most analysis is second-hand from South Korean, Japanese and Taiwanese outlets.
items.op: A summit that reshapes regional security should not be settled in closed rooms. When a joint declaration says nothing about the Korean Peninsula or Taiwan, while the people there watch the outcome, transparency is the minimum owed.
